title: C#
summary: Microsoft's modern, typed language for .NET apps, web APIs, Windows tools and Unity games.

lessons.title: C#: syntax basics

concept.text:
C# (say 'see sharp') is a statically typed language that runs on .NET. It looks a lot like Java but has more shortcuts, such as `var` to let the compiler infer a type and `$"..."` strings to insert values.

Modern C# lets you write statements at the top of a file with no class or `Main` method, which is ideal for learning.
concept.analogy: If Java is a manual car, C# is the same car with power steering and cruise control. The same engine and rules of the road, with more comfort features.

steps.title: Variables
steps.text: Declare a type, or use `var` when the type is obvious from the value.

steps.title: Print with interpolation
steps.text: A `$` before the string lets you put expressions inside braces.

steps.title: Branch and loop
steps.text: The syntax matches Java and JavaScript.
steps.code:
if (score >= 10) Console.WriteLine("Level up!");
for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) Console.WriteLine(i);

steps.title: Create and run a project
steps.text: Install the .NET SDK, then use the dotnet command.
steps.code:
dotnet new console -o Hello
cd Hello
dotnet run

challenge.prompt: Write a program that prints the multiplication table for 7, from `7 x 1 = 7` to `7 x 10 = 70`.
challenge.hint: Loop `i` from 1 to 10 and use an interpolated string with `{7 * i}` inside it.

takeaways: C# is statically typed and runs on .NET.
String interpolation with $"..." keeps output code readable.
dotnet new, dotnet run and dotnet build are the core commands.

lessons.title: C#: classes, properties and LINQ

concept.text:
C# classes use **properties**: fields with built-in get and set logic, written in one line. For data-only types, a `record` gives you a constructor, equality and printing for free.

**LINQ** is C#'s standout feature: query any collection with methods like `Where`, `Select` and `OrderBy`, in the same spirit as SQL.
concept.analogy: LINQ is a conveyor belt with stations. Items roll past a filter station (Where), a reshaping station (Select) and a sorting station (OrderBy), and a finished batch comes off the end.

steps.title: Declare a record
steps.text: One line creates a full, immutable data type.

steps.title: Write a class with properties
steps.text: `private set` means only the class itself can change the value.

steps.title: Query with LINQ
steps.text: The arrow `=>` defines a small inline function called a lambda.

challenge.prompt: Given `var prices = new List<decimal> { 60m, 220m, 25m, 15m };`, use LINQ to print the total of all prices above 20.

takeaways: Properties wrap fields with get and set in one line.
Records are concise, immutable data types.
LINQ filters, sorts and transforms collections with chained methods.

lessons.title: C# mini project: an inventory tracker

concept.text: Build a small inventory tracker: a list of items, a low-stock report and a total stock value. It uses records, a list and LINQ together, which is the core of most line-of-business .NET code.
concept.analogy: You are the stockroom manager with a clipboard. The list is your clipboard, and each LINQ query is a question you would ask it: what is running low, and what is everything worth?

steps.title: Model an item
steps.text: A record with a name, quantity and unit price.

steps.title: Report low stock
steps.text: Filter with `Where`, then loop over the result to print.

steps.title: Total the value
steps.text: `Sum` takes a lambda so you can multiply quantity by price for each item. The `:C` format prints currency.

interactive.expected:
Low stock:
  Monitor (3 left)
  Mouse (2 left)
Total value: 1430

challenge.prompt: Print the single most valuable line of stock (highest `Qty * Price`) as `Most valuable: Keyboard`.

takeaways: Records plus List<T> model most business data.
LINQ answers questions about collections without manual loops.
Use decimal, not double, for money.
